strengths: Well-motivated and timely research addressing a key limitation of existing code generation benchmarks—specifically, the lack of explicit domain knowledge corpora to evaluate how LLMs learn and adapt to unfamiliar software frameworks.

Highly rigorous benchmark construction process involving 28.5 person-months of effort, with multi-granularity requirement specifications and execution-based validation (using unit and integration tests inside Docker environments).
Comprehensive and diverse coverage of modern, highly relevant domains such as Reinforcement Learning (VeRL, Open-R1), Agents (Smolagents), and RAG (GraphRAG).
Extensive experimental evaluation of a wide range of state-of-the-art LLMs, domain adaptation methods (SFT, RAG, kNN-LM), and coding agents (Claude Code, SWE-agent, OpenHands).

Insightful analysis of training dynamics, particularly the negative scaling of corpus size for parameter-efficient fine-tuning and the catastrophic forgetting observed during cross-domain continual learning.
weaknesses: The dataset scale for the Domain Knowledge Understanding task is relatively small (107 Q&A pairs total across 11 frameworks), which might limit the statistical significance of evaluations on this subtask.
The definition of 'domain knowledge' in the code generation task heavily focuses on API compliance and syntax details of specific libraries rather than deep domain-level algorithmic reasoning.

While the paper analyzes several training-based adaptation baselines, the training strategy used (concatenating raw files with end-of-text tokens) is quite basic; exploring more advanced structured code-pretraining or instruction-tuning strategies in the main paper would strengthen the analysis of specialization limits.

strengths: Highly novel and well-motivated benchmark design that explicitly pairs domain knowledge corpora with test suites, directly addressing a key gap in evaluating domain specialization methods (such as SFT, RAG, and kNN-LM) in software engineering.

Broad and realistic coverage of 6 emerging, cutting-edge AI domains (e.g., Reinforcement Learning, Agents, RAG) with 11 software frameworks and 25 projects, ensuring the tasks are highly relevant and representative of real-world development challenges.

Rigorous benchmark construction process with extensive human effort (28.5 person-months), incorporating execution-based test validation (averaging 8.6 unit tests per function) and systematic data contamination detection to ensure high quality and reliability.

In-depth, multi-dimensional empirical evaluations involving 10 SOTA base models, diverse domain specialization baselines, and advanced agent systems, accompanied by highly insightful analyses (e.g., negative scaling behavior of corpus size for SFT, knowledge conflict in continual learning, and detailed error categorization).
weaknesses: The domain knowledge understanding task relies on multiple-choice Q&A, which is highly verifiable but may not fully capture the interactive, free-form query style that software developers exhibit when consulting technical documentation in practice.

The training-based domain specialization baselines (such as full-parameter SFT on large framework codebases) require non-trivial computational resources, which might hinder easy replication and baseline development for resource-constrained research groups.

Quantitative evaluation of full project-level code generation remains limited in the main text due to high cost and complexity, with most of the systematic benchmarking focused on core function generation.

strengths: Innovative Benchmark Design: Unlike existing code benchmarks that only evaluate pre-existing model knowledge, KoCo-Bench pairs domain knowledge corpora (documentation, source code, examples) with test sets. This enables a realistic evaluation of how domain specialization methods (SFT, RAG, etc.) help models acquire and apply new knowledge.

Rigorous Construction & Evaluation: The benchmark is built on 11 frameworks and 25 projects, verified via unit and integration tests in Docker environments to ensure correctness. It also includes 107 curated multi-choice Q&A tasks.

Comprehensive Baselines: Evaluates 10 LLMs alongside major specialization techniques (SFT, LoRA, RAG, kNN-LM) and agentic systems (Claude Code, SWE-Agent, OpenHands), showing a highly complete empirical picture.

Deep and Actionable Analysis: The paper provides highly interesting findings, such as the negative scaling correlation of SFT/LoRA with knowledge corpus size, cross-domain catastrophic forgetting, and detailed categorization of API misuse errors.
weaknesses: Small Q&A Sample Size: The domain knowledge understanding task contains only 107 multiple-choice questions, which is relatively small and might have higher variance in performance metrics.

High Execution Costs: Repro-level evaluation of advanced coding agents (such as Claude Code) consumes a massive number of tokens (averaging over 619k tokens per sample as shown in Figure 5), posing a steep financial and computational barrier for standard academic reproduction.

Clarification on Corpus Chunking: The details on how the knowledge corpus was processed (e.g., chunking strategy, file ordering, and filtering out of target solutions to prevent leakage during RAG/SFT) could be more explicitly documented to ensure perfect reproducibility.
